segments.title: The 1801 precedent at Copenhagen
segments.body: The first Battle of Copenhagen in 1801 provides the comparison for the 1807 expedition. Admiral Parker commanded the earlier force, with Admiral Lord Nelson as his second in command. The opening recap describes Danish ships at Copenhagen as captured or destroyed. Six years later, British forces returned to the Danish capital to seize warships again.

evidence.note: The transcript recaps Parker, Nelson, and Danish ships captured or destroyed at Copenhagen.
The closing comparison explicitly dates the two attacks to 1801 and 1807.

segments.summary: Parker and Nelson's attack in 1801 introduces the comparison with Britain's return to Copenhagen six years later.

segments.title: Gambier and Cathcart return to Copenhagen in 1807
segments.body: Six years after the first attack, Admiral James Gambier and General William Cathcart are sent against Copenhagen. Their expedition brings an army alongside the Royal Navy, with Arthur Wellesley among the officers taking part. The account describes British forces storming in and taking the Danish fleet. It compares this result with the earlier loss of Danish ships at the capital.

evidence.note: Admiral James Gambier, General William Cathcart, and Arthur Wellesley took part in the second capture of the Danish fleet. The garbled name at 1:00 refers to Cathcart, based on his command alongside Gambier and corroboration from the National Army Museum: https://www.nam.ac.uk/explore/copenhagen-expedition-1807.

segments.summary: Admiral James Gambier and General William Cathcart lead the naval and army forces sent against Copenhagen in 1807.

segments.title: James Gambier's Ohio town and college connection
segments.body: James Gambier's introduction links him with the founding of a town in Ohio. He also supported a college there as one of its founding benefactors. The town and college are not named in this brief aside.

evidence.note: The introduction identifies James Gambier, says he helps found a town in Ohio, and describes him as one of a college's founding benefactors. Neither institution nor town is named.

segments.summary: Gambier's introduction includes his connection with an Ohio town and his support for a college there.

segments.title: Wellesley's separate land battle during the Copenhagen expedition
segments.body: Arthur Wellesley is among the army officers accompanying the 1807 naval expedition. He fights a separate battle against Danish troops some distance from Copenhagen. Its purpose is described as stopping those troops from leaving Copenhagen. The brief account gives no battle name or further explanation of these troop movements.

evidence.note: Wellesley accompanies the army and fights Danish troops further away. The wording at 1:26-1:28 says this stops them leaving Copenhagen, but does not clarify the movements. The public note preserves this limitation without inferring that the army held Danish troops away from the fleet.

segments.summary: Arthur Wellesley fights Danish troops away from Copenhagen as part of the army accompanying the 1807 naval expedition.

segments.title: Why Britain repeated the Copenhagen attack
segments.body: Denmark's alignment with France is given as the reason for the British attacks in both 1801 and 1807. The Royal Navy's repeated arrival at Copenhagen and seizure of Danish ships form the closing comparison, twice within less than a decade. The account ends with the blunt warning that Denmark should not join the French.

evidence.note: The British attacks of 1801 and 1807 support the closing warning that Denmark should not join the French.

segments.summary: The closing comparison links the attacks of 1801 and 1807 to British opposition to Denmark joining France.
